verdict: OK to lend in Mehsana engineering and capital goods, but only to order-backed fabricators and component makers with clean receivables; avoid EPC and working-capital-heavy contractors.
title: Mehsana Engineering & Capital Goods: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
Value sits in the order book and the customer approval, not in the machines. **So when a proposal lands, check the order book quality first; if orders are single-customer or verbal, ask for the purchase order file and last twelve months of dispatches.**

## Where cash sits and what has changed
**Working capital is the whole business: inventory of raw tube and plate, then receivables from large buyers who pay on their own terms.** Rating commentary on capital goods notes payables have supported the cycle for two fiscals, and that EPC players carry a longer cash conversion cycle than OEMs [11]; ICRA's methodology makes the same point, that a longer cycle means more funding needed [9]. **So structure limits against the assessed cycle, not the requested one; if the customer asks for more, ask for the receivable ageing by buyer.** Locally, the Ahmedabad-Mehsana eight-lane plan was launched with Rs 2,600 Cr of stone laid [2], though the GRICL toll concession runs to 2033 and the firm has asked to extend to 2040 [1] — that is construction demand, not yet a factory order. **Pursue tier-2 suppliers to that plant and to process-equipment OEMs; avoid pure labour-contract fabricators with no own machinery.** Peer results show the demand is real but margins are not automatic: DEE's revenue rose 77% YoY to Rs 286.7 crore with operating profit at Rs 47.6 crore [5], while Suzlon grew revenue 26% to Rs 4,869 crore but EBITDA margin narrowed to 14.8% from 18.6% [7]. ## How to grow safely
**Lend against purchase orders and receivables, not against projected capacity.** Take monthly stock and receivable statements, quarterly GST returns, and a monthly order-book position. **If a borrower's receivable days cross the sanctioned cycle, ask for the buyer-wise ageing and stop fresh disbursal until it clears.** For capex, insist on a term loan matched to the asset with a moratorium tied to commissioning, not to sales. ## Early warning signs
**Watch for order book that grows while dispatches stay flat, and for bank guarantees used for bidding rather than performance.** ICRA notes bid and performance guarantees are a normal working-capital demand in these businesses [9], so track guarantee exposure monthly. **If guarantee limits are fully drawn and receivables are ageing, treat it as a cash problem, not a growth problem.**
watch: Receivable days exceed sanctioned cycle for two months -> freeze fresh disbursal and seek buyer-wise ageing
